abstract: |
  Classic psychedelics are thought to relax prior expectations, which should weaken visual illusions. Evidence is scarce, especially outside the acute state, and error rates, the usual measure of illusion sensitivity, also depend on overall performance. We tested 117 adults, of whom 43 had never used a classic psychedelic, 39 had used one within the last 30 days (the "afterglow" period) and 35 longer ago. They completed the Illusion Game, a response-time task of judging which of two targets is larger while the strength of an illusion (Ebbinghaus, Müller-Lyer, vertical-horizontal) varies independently of the real difference between them. A hierarchical drift diffusion model was fitted to every choice and response time. Both user groups set wider decision boundaries than naïve participants, gathering more evidence before responding, and made fewer errors. We then computed an index of illusion sensitivity independent of overall accuracy: the effect of illusion strength on performance relative to that of the real difference. This index was 22% lower in users on average, equally in recent and past users, and unrelated to age, language, student status, psychological flexibility, distress or the intensity of the last experience. It correlated moderately across illusions, less than general performance did. Psychedelic users appeared somewhat less sensitive to illusions, as relaxed priors would predict, but the absence of a clear link with use recency limits interpretative confidence and generalizability.

```{r}
library(patchwork)

# Renders from paper/ (quarto) or from the repo root (interactively).

res <- function(file) read.csv(file.path(root, "analysis/results", file))
averaged <- res("ddm_groups_averaged.csv")
contrasts <- res("ddm_groups_contrasts.csv")
slopes <- res("ddm_groups_slopes.csv")
correlates <- res("ddm_correlates.csv")
correlations <- res("ddm_correlations.csv")
curves <- res("ddm_groups_means.csv")
ppc_curves <- res("ddm_ppc_curves.csv")

questionnaires <- read.csv(file.path(root, "data/questionnaires.csv"))
trials <- read.csv(file.path(root, "data/data_illusiongame.csv"))
# The group-level parameters (posterior medians) at the condition that Figure
# 2A draws: the strongest conflicting Ebbinghaus illusion, at mid difficulty.
# mu is the drift towards the error boundary and delta = -mu the drift towards
# the correct one; bias is the start point as a share of the boundary
# separation, from the correct boundary.
ddm_par <- with(curves[curves$Illusion_Type == "Ebbinghaus" & curves$Illusion_Strength == 1 & curves$Task_Difficulty == 0, ],
                tapply(Median, list(Group, Quantity), function(v) v))
stopifnot(dim(ddm_par) == c(3, 7))

group_col <- c(Never = "#7a7a75", Past = "#2a78d6", Recent = "#00dcff")

group_lab <- c(Never = "Psychedelic-naïve", Past = "Past users", Recent = "Recent users")
contrast_lab <- c("Past - Never" = "Past − Naïve", "Recent - Never" = "Recent − Naïve", "Recent - Past" = "Recent − Past")
illusions <- c(Ebbinghaus = "Ebbinghaus", MullerLyer = "Müller-Lyer", VerticalHorizontal = "Vertical-horizontal")

# One row of a results table, and its "median [low, high]".
pick <- function(df, ...) {
  cond <- list(...)
  for (n in names(cond)) df <- df[df[[n]] == cond[[n]], ]
  stopifnot(nrow(df) == 1)
  df
}
minus <- function(s) gsub("-", "−", s, fixed = TRUE)
fmt <- function(x, digits = 2) minus(sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f [%.", digits, "f, %.", digits, "f]"), x$Median, x$CI_low, x$CI_high))
ms <- function(x) minus(sprintf("%+.0f ms [%+.0f, %+.0f]", 1000 * x$Median, 1000 * x$CI_low, 1000 * x$CI_high))
pts <- function(x) {
  unit <- if (abs(round(100 * x$Median)) == 1) "point" else "points"
  minus(sprintf("%+.0f %s [%+.0f, %+.0f]", 100 * x$Median, unit, 100 * x$CI_low, 100 * x$CI_high))
}
avg <- function(q, contrast, ill = "All") pick(averaged, Quantity = q, Contrast = contrast, Illusion_Type = ill)
eff <- function(q, contrast, ill) pick(contrasts, Quantity = q, Contrast = contrast, Illusion_Type = ill,
                                       Measure = "Effect of the illusion (strength 0 to 1)")
idx <- function(group, ill) pick(slopes[slopes$Quantity == "index" & !is.na(slopes$Group), ], Group = group, Illusion_Type = ill)
idx_c <- function(contrast, ill) pick(slopes[slopes$Quantity == "index" & !is.na(slopes$Contrast), ], Contrast = contrast, Illusion_Type = ill)
# How much smaller each user group's illusion is, in percent of the naive
# value, per group and illusion (the abstract's rounded numbers come from it).
idx_pct <- unlist(lapply(c("Past - Never", "Recent - Never"), function(cn) {
  sapply(c("Ebbinghaus", "MullerLyer", "VerticalHorizontal"), function(ill) {
    -100 * idx_c(cn, ill)$Median / idx("Never", ill)$Median
  })
}))
cov <- function(q, design, term) pick(correlates, Quantity = q, Design = design, Term = term)
cor_mag <- function(pair) fmt(pick(correlations, Quantity = "Illusion magnitude (strength / difficulty)", Pair = pair))
# A contrast's medians across illusions, and their range as text ("-0.52 to -0.43").
eff_all <- function(q, contrast, ill = names(illusions)) sapply(ill, function(il) eff(q, contrast, il)$Median)
idx_all <- function(contrast) sapply(names(illusions), function(il) idx_c(contrast, il)$Median)
med_rng <- function(v, digits = 2) minus(paste(sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f"), range(v)), collapse = " to "))
# The Results say that, one illusion at a time, the 95% intervals of all six of
# the magnitude's user - naive contrasts exclude zero.
idx_below <- sapply(c("Past - Never", "Recent - Never"), function(cn) sapply(names(illusions), function(il) idx_c(cn, il)$CI_high < 0))
stopifnot(all(idx_below))
# The other qualitative claims of the Results, which a refit could change:
# whether a 95% interval includes zero.
ci0 <- function(x) x$CI_low < 0 & x$CI_high > 0
vs_naive <- c("Past - Never", "Recent - Never")
stopifnot(
  # General performance: wider boundaries and fewer errors in both user groups,
  # a non-decision time that is not reliably longer, a higher drift rate in
  # recent users only, no difference in start point or drift variability.
  !any(sapply(vs_naive, function(cn) ci0(avg("boundary", cn)) | ci0(avg("perror", cn)))),
  all(sapply(vs_naive, function(cn) ci0(avg("ndt", cn)))),
  !ci0(avg("delta", "Recent - Never")), !ci0(avg("delta", "Recent - Past")), ci0(avg("delta", "Past - Never")),
  all(sapply(c(vs_naive, "Recent - Past"), function(cn) ci0(avg("bias", cn)) & ci0(avg("sigmadrift", cn)))),
  # Illusion sensitivity: the illusion's effect on discriminability does not
  # differ from naive on any illusion; on errors, not on the Muller-Lyer.
  all(sapply(vs_naive, function(cn) sapply(names(illusions), function(il) ci0(eff("delta", cn, il))))),
  all(sapply(vs_naive, function(cn) ci0(eff("perror", cn, "MullerLyer")))),
  # ... on the Ebbinghaus it does, on the vertical-horizontal it does not.
  !any(sapply(vs_naive, function(cn) ci0(eff("perror", cn, "Ebbinghaus")))),
  all(sapply(vs_naive, function(cn) ci0(eff("perror", cn, "VerticalHorizontal"))))
)
# And those of the age paragraphs: with age in the regression, the
# non-decision time and past users' error rate no longer differ from naive,
# while the boundaries and recent users' error rate and drift rate still do.
age_adj <- function(q, cn) cov(q, "Group + age", cn)
stopifnot(
  all(sapply(vs_naive, function(cn) ci0(age_adj("Non-decision time (s), no illusion", cn)))),
  !any(sapply(vs_naive, function(cn) ci0(age_adj("Boundary, no illusion", cn)))),
  ci0(age_adj("P(error), no illusion", "Past - Never")), !ci0(age_adj("P(error), no illusion", "Recent - Never")),
  !ci0(age_adj("Discriminability, no illusion", "Recent - Never"))
)

# Psychedelic use by degree, among users: neither the illusion magnitude nor
# the boundary follows the time since the last use or the lifetime number of
# uses.
use_days <- function(q) cov(q, "Days since last use (users)", "Days since last use (per tenfold)")
use_life <- function(q) cov(q, "Group + lifetime use (users)", "Lifetime use (per category)")
stopifnot(ci0(use_days("Illusion magnitude (strength / difficulty)")), ci0(use_life("Illusion magnitude (strength / difficulty)")),
          ci0(use_days("Boundary, no illusion")), ci0(use_life("Boundary, no illusion")))
# The exclusions listed in the Participants section (2 + 3 + 3 + 1 + 1), and
# the three past users classified from the yes/no question.
no_days <- groups[groups$Group != "Never" & is.na(groups$Days), ]
stopifnot(nrow(participants) - nrow(groups) == 10, nrow(no_days) == 3, no_days$Group == "Past", no_days$Psychedelics_LastMonth == "No")
# The reduction of the illusion magnitude in users per illusion (percent of the
# naive value, averaged over the two user groups).
idx_pct_ill <- tapply(idx_pct, names(idx_pct), mean)
stopifnot(setequal(names(idx_pct_ill), names(illusions)))

n_group <- table(factor(groups$Group, levels = names(group_col)))
n_trials <- nrow(trials)
# Asterisks: the probability of direction at the thresholds that match
# p < .05, .01 and .001 (pd = 1 - p / 2).
stars <- function(pd) ifelse(pd >= 0.9995, "***", ifelse(pd >= 0.995, "**", ifelse(pd >= 0.975, "*", "")))
```

# Introduction

Classic psychedelics such as psilocybin, LSD and DMT act on serotonin 2A (5-HT2A) receptors and alter perception, cognition and self-experience [@vollenweider2020psychedelic]. An influential account of how they do so is the relaxed beliefs under psychedelics (REBUS) model. It holds that 5-HT2A agonism makes high-level prior expectations less precise, so that perception relies more on sensory evidence and less on what is expected [@carhartharris2019rebus; @clark2013whatever]. Geometrical illusions are often explained by such priors: expectations about the layout of the world are applied to a display that violates them [@gregory1997knowledge; @howe2005muller]. To the extent that an illusion depends on such high-level priors, REBUS predicts that psychedelics should weaken it. That extent is not established and may differ from one illusion to another, as geometrical illusions have also been related to earlier stages of visual processing [@morgan1990biases; @schwarzkopf2011surface]. The same reasoning has been applied to schizophrenia, where a reduced susceptibility to some illusions, though debated, is attributed to weakened priors [@notredame2014visual; @king2017review].

The evidence on illusions is thin and inconsistent. Under acute psilocybin, the Ebbinghaus illusion became *larger* while surround suppression in early visual cortex decreased [@aqil2025psilocybin]. Surround suppression of contrast was enhanced at the peak of psilocybin in one pilot trial [@swanson2024enhanced] and unchanged under low-dose LSD in another [@jaeckel2026lowdose].

Whether psychedelics weaken illusions beyond the acute state is a separate question, and one of practical interest. The relaxation of priors has been proposed as the mechanism by which psychedelics benefit mental health [@carhartharris2019rebus], and these benefits, like changes in personality and attitudes, have been documented long after one or a few doses [@aday2020longterm; @knudsen2023sustained]. A subacute "afterglow" lasting days to weeks has also been described after psychedelic use, with changes in mood, openness and cognitive flexibility [@evens2023afterglow], and animal work reports relaxed predictive processing in visual cortex for days after a single dose [@west2026psychedelics]. If relaxed priors outlast the acute state, their perceptual consequences should too. Yet experienced users, who reported lasting changes in self-experience, did not differ from controls on a bodily illusion [@harduf2023bodily], and to our knowledge no study has measured classic geometrical illusions in psychedelic users outside the acute state.

Measuring susceptibility to illusions is not straightforward either, because illusion paradigms are prone to conflating the illusion with other effects. Subjective ratings and adjustment procedures can reflect metacognitive judgements and response criteria as well as perception, and error rates can reflect perceptual discrimination and overall task performance. In autistic children, for instance, a group difference in susceptibility to the Müller-Lyer illusion appeared with a method of adjustment, but not with same-different judgements or with a forced choice designed to minimise decision biases, and was attributed to the criterion for responding rather than to perception [@manning2017susceptibility].

The Illusion Game is a paradigm that tries to accommodate these issues [@makowski2021parametric; @makowski2023novel], with three advantages over classical procedures. First, the judgement is objective and speeded. Participants indicate which of two targets is bigger or longer as fast as they can, every trial has a correct answer, and the illusion is measured by what it does to accuracy and response times, not by a rating or an adjustment of how large it appears. Second, each stimulus is generated from two parameters that vary independently and continuously. The *task difficulty* is the real (objective) difference between the two targets: the smaller the difference, the harder the trial. The *illusion strength* is the magnitude of the context that biases how the targets look, and this context can work in favour of the real difference, which makes the task easier, or against it, which makes it harder. The effect of the illusion can therefore be separated from the ability to tell the targets apart. Third, choices and response times can be modelled together with an evidence accumulation model [@ratcliff2008diffusion], which describes performance by a few parameters and estimates how each of them changes with the illusion separately from its level without one. In addition to these parameters, we computed an index to facilitate comparisons between groups that differ in average performance. Because the real difference varies as well, the effect of the illusion can be expressed relative to that of the real difference, that is, as the real difference that the illusion is equivalent to. We call this index the *illusion magnitude*.

Here we compared adults who had never used a classic psychedelic with two groups of users, split by whether their last use was within the preceding 30 days, the window used in the afterglow literature [@evens2023afterglow]. All completed the Illusion Game with three illusions (Ebbinghaus, Müller-Lyer and vertical-horizontal), <!-- TODO (Marco's comment): say why these three illusions were chosen. --> and a hierarchical drift diffusion model was fitted to every trial. We examined all of the model's parameters, to describe how the groups differ in general performance as well as in illusion sensitivity. If the relaxation of priors outlasts the acute state and then fades, as the afterglow suggests, the illusions should affect recent users less than naïve participants, and past users should fall in between. We report the effect of the illusions on how well the targets are told apart (their discriminability) and on errors, together with the illusion magnitude. As the groups were recruited through different routes and differed in other characteristics, we additionally tested whether age, language, student status, psychological flexibility or distress account for the differences observed, and whether, among users, these differences follow the intensity of the last psychedelic experience, the time since it or the lifetime number of uses.

# Methods

## Participants

Participants were recruited online, in French or in English, for a study of psychedelic experience, perception and cognition, which also included a self-association task not reported in the current study. Psychedelic users were reached through psychedelic societies and related online communities, and psychedelic-naïve participants through word of mouth and the researchers' social media. All participants were at least 18 years old, took part on a desktop or laptop computer, gave informed consent and were not paid. The Ethics Committee of Université Paris Cité approved the study (IRB No. 00012023-105).

Sessions ran from March 2024 to April 2026, when the data were frozen. Of the `r nrow(participants)` sessions in the four recruitment arms, `r nrow(participants) - nrow(groups)` were excluded before analysis: two did not reach the end of the protocol, three were tested after the data freeze, three controls reported having used a classic psychedelic, one user reported experience only with non-classic substances, and one control stated an age of 16. The analysed sample comprises `r sum(n_group)` adults in three mutually exclusive groups: `r n_group[["Never"]]` who had never taken a classic psychedelic (psychedelic-naïve; Naïve in contrasts), `r n_group[["Recent"]]` whose last classic psychedelic was 30 days ago or less (recent users; Recent) and `r n_group[["Past"]]` whose last was more than 30 days before the session (past users; Past). Users were assigned to these two groups according to the number of days since their last use, which they gave as free text. Three users gave a date or no number, and were assigned to the past users because they answered no to a yes/no question about use in the last month.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sample
#| apa-twocolumn: true
#| tbl-cap: "The three groups."
#| apa-note: "Values are n (%) unless stated. Native: native speaker of the language the session ran in. Diagnosis: self-reported past or current psychiatric diagnosis. Meditation: at least once a week. AAQ-II: 7 to 49, higher means less psychological flexibility. DASS-21: total, 0 to 3, higher means more distress (see Questionnaires)."
included <- merge(groups[c("Participant", "Group", "Days")], participants)
included <- merge(included, questionnaires[c("Participant", "AAQ", "DASS_Total", "MEQ_Total", "MEQ_Complete")], all.x = TRUE)
stopifnot(nrow(included) == nrow(groups))
included$Group <- factor(included$Group, levels = names(group_col))
pct <- function(x) sprintf("%d (%.0f%%)", sum(x, na.rm = TRUE), 100 * mean(x, na.rm = TRUE))
mean_sd <- function(x, digits = 1) sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f (%.", digits, "f)"), mean(x, na.rm = TRUE), sd(x, na.rm = TRUE))
describe <- function(g) {
  age <- g$Age
  c("N" = nrow(g),
    "Age, mean (SD)" = sprintf("%.1f (%.1f)", mean(age, na.rm = TRUE), sd(age, na.rm = TRUE)),
    "Age, median (range)" = sprintf("%g (%g-%g)", median(age, na.rm = TRUE), min(age, na.rm = TRUE), max(age, na.rm = TRUE)),
    "Women" = pct(g$Sex == "Female"),
    "Students" = pct(g$Student == "Yes"),
    "Native speakers" = pct(g$Language_Level == "Native"),
    "Session in English" = pct(g$Session_Language == "English"),
    # Labels kept to 19 characters: a longer one pushes the markdown table
    # past pandoc's 72 columns, and its cells then wrap.
    "Postgraduate degree" = pct(g$Education %in% c("Master", "Doctorate")),
    "Past diagnosis" = pct(g$Diagnosis_Past == "Yes"),
    "Current diagnosis" = pct(g$Diagnosis_Current == "Yes"),
    "Meditation" = pct(g$Meditation == "Yes"),
    "AAQ-II, mean (SD)" = mean_sd(g$AAQ),
    "DASS-21, mean (SD)" = mean_sd(g$DASS_Total, 2))
}
tab1 <- sapply(split(included, included$Group), describe)
# For the Discussion: how many of each group are aged 31 to 50.
age_mid <- tapply(included$Age, included$Group, function(a) sum(a >= 31 & a <= 50, na.rm = TRUE))
stopifnot(age_mid[["Never"]] == 1)
knitr::kable(tab1, col.names = group_lab[colnames(tab1)])
```

@tbl-sample describes the groups. The naïve participants were about twelve years younger than both user groups, were mostly students and women, and fewer than half were native speakers of the language of their session. The two user groups were similar on all of these, and the three groups had similar questionnaire scores. The groups therefore differ in recruitment route, age, student status and language as well as in psychedelic use. How the analysis deals with this is described under Participant-level analyses.

```{r}
#| tbl-cap: "Psychedelic use in the two user groups."

Lifetime use: number of occasions, chosen among seven categories from never to more than 100 times; one past user answered \"never\" but described a last experience with ayahuasca, and is in none of the three rows. Dose and intention: of the last classic psychedelic experience, as judged by the participant. Other substance: any other substance taken during that experience. MEQ-30: Mystical Experience Questionnaire, about that experience (0 to 5); complete: at least 3 on each of its four factors."
users <- droplevels(included[included$Group != "Never", ])
users$Other_Substance <- rowSums(users[grep("^Drug_", names(users))] == "Yes", na.rm = TRUE) > 0
iqr <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f (%.0f–%.0f)", median(x, na.rm = TRUE), quantile(x, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE), quantile(x, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE))
describe_use <- function(g) {
  freq <- g$Psychedelics_Frequency
  subst <- g$Experience_Substance
  dose <- g$Experience_Dose
  aim <- g$Experience_Intention
  c("N" = nrow(g),
    "Days since last use, median (IQR)" = iqr(g$Days),
    "Lifetime use: 1 to 10 times" = pct(freq %in% c("One time", "Between 2 and 5 times", "Between 6 and 10 times")),
    "Lifetime use: 11 to 50 times" = pct(freq %in% "Between 11 and 50 times"),
    "Lifetime use: more than 50 times" = pct(freq %in% c("Between 51 and 100 times", "More than 100 times")),
    "Last substance: psilocybin" = pct(subst %in% "Psilocybin/mushrooms/truffles"),
    "Last substance: LSD or analogue" = pct(subst %in% "LSD/1P-LSD/ALD-52"),
    "Last substance: DMT or ayahuasca" = pct(subst %in% c("N,N-DMT", "5-MeO-DMT (Bufo)", "Ayahuasca")),
    "Dose: lower than typical" = pct(dose %in% c("Very low", "Lower than a typical dose")),
    "Dose: typical" = pct(dose %in% "Typical"),
    "Dose: higher than typical" = pct(dose %in% c("Higher than a typical dose", "Very high")),
    "Intention: recreational" = pct(aim %in% "Recreational"),
    "Intention: therapeutic" = pct(aim %in% "Therapeutic"),
    "Intention: spiritual or religious" = pct(aim %in% "Spiritual/religious"),
    "Intention: curiosity or other" = pct(aim %in% c("Curiosity", "Microdosing", "Other")),
    "Other substance at the same time" = pct(g$Other_Substance),
    "MEQ-30 total, mean (SD)" = mean_sd(g$MEQ_Total, 2),
    "Complete mystical experience" = pct(g$MEQ_Complete))
}
tab_use <- sapply(split(users, users$Group), describe_use)
knitr::kable(tab_use, col.names = group_lab[colnames(tab_use)])
# For the text.
use_pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * mean(x))
days <- split(users$Days, users$Group)
days_txt <- function(d) if (d >= 730) sprintf("%.0f years", d / 365.25) else sprintf("%.0f days", d)
```

@tbl-use describes the users' psychedelic use, as they reported it. `r use_pct(users$Psychedelics_Frequency %in% c("Between 11 and 50 times", "Between 51 and 100 times", "More than 100 times"))` had used a classic psychedelic more than ten times in their life. Their last experience was with psilocybin for `r use_pct(users$Experience_Substance %in% "Psilocybin/mushrooms/truffles")` and with LSD or an analogue for `r use_pct(users$Experience_Substance %in% "LSD/1P-LSD/ALD-52")`, and `r use_pct(users$Other_Substance)` had taken another substance with it, most often cannabis or alcohol. Recent users had last used a median of `r sprintf("%.0f", median(days$Recent, na.rm = TRUE))` days before the session (range `r min(days$Recent, na.rm = TRUE)` to `r max(days$Recent, na.rm = TRUE)`), and past users a median of `r sprintf("%.0f", median(days$Past, na.rm = TRUE))` days (range `r days_txt(min(days$Past, na.rm = TRUE))` to `r days_txt(max(days$Past, na.rm = TRUE))`). The two user groups reported similar doses and intentions. Recent users had used more often in their life than past users, and LSD was more often their last substance.

## The Illusion Game

Participants completed a shortened online version of the Illusion Game [@makowski2023novel] with three illusions (@fig-data A), generated with Pyllusion [@makowski2021parametric]. In the Ebbinghaus illusion, two red circles are shown side by side, each surrounded by black circles, and the participant says which red circle is bigger. A circle surrounded by large circles looks smaller, so the illusion strength is the relative size of the surrounding circles. In the Müller-Lyer illusion, two horizontal red lines are shown one above the other, with black fins at their ends, and the participant says which line is longer. The illusion strength is the angle of the fins: the more they are tilted, the stronger the illusion. In the vertical-horizontal illusion, two red lines are shown side by side, one of them rotated towards the vertical, and the participant says which is longer. Lines closer to the vertical look longer, so the illusion strength is the angle of rotation: the larger the rotation, the stronger the illusion. In each illusion, the context biases the apparent difference between the targets in one direction. It can work in favour of the real difference, exaggerating it and making the discrimination easier (a *facilitating* illusion), or against it, making the discrimination harder (a *conflicting* illusion). The illusion is present in both cases, and only its direction relative to the real difference changes.

Each trial began with a fixation cross lasting 600 to 1,100 ms, followed by the stimulus, which stayed on screen until the participant pressed one of two arrow keys. Participants were asked to respond as fast as possible without making errors. Each illusion had a practice block of 8 trials and two test blocks of 80 trials, which gives 480 test trials in all. Trials were in random order within a block. The order of the illusions (Müller-Lyer, Ebbinghaus, vertical-horizontal) was the same in both series of test blocks and for every participant, so that it cannot differ between the groups. After each test block, participants were shown a score combining their speed and accuracy (derived from their mean correct response time divided by their proportion of correct responses). The Illusion Game followed the self-association task, and the AAQ-II and DASS-21 (see Questionnaires) were completed between its first and second series of test blocks.

Each illusion used 20 illusion strengths (10 facilitating and 10 conflicting) and 8 real differences, split between its two blocks. The real difference is relative: the larger target exceeded the smaller one by 5 to 50% in the Ebbinghaus illusion, by 4.5 to 45% in the Müller-Lyer illusion and by 3 to 30% in the vertical-horizontal illusion. At the strongest illusions, the surrounding circles were 150% larger than the circle they surrounded, the fins were tilted by 30 degrees and the line was rotated by 45 degrees. The stimuli were images of 800 by 800 pixels, shown at that size in full-screen mode. Their physical size therefore depended on the display, but the real differences, being relative, did not.

Both predictors were normalized: Illusion strength runs from −1 (the strongest facilitating illusion) through 0 (no illusion) to +1 (the strongest conflicting illusion). Task difficulty runs from −1 (the largest difference shown, the easiest trials) to +1 (the smallest, the hardest trials), so that the whole range of difficulty spans 2 units.

## Questionnaires

```{r}
#| label: alpha
items <- function(pattern) participants[grep(pattern, names(participants))]
alpha <- function(x) {
  x <- x[stats::complete.cases(x), ]
  k <- ncol(x)
  k / (k - 1) * (1 - sum(apply(x, 2, stats::var)) / stats::var(rowSums(x)))
}
a <- sapply(c(AAQ = "^AAQ_", DASS = "^DASS_", Depression = "^DASS_Depression_", Anxiety = "^DASS_Anxiety_",
              Stress = "^DASS_Stress_", MEQ = "^MEQ_", Mystical = "^MEQ_Mystical_", PositiveMood = "^MEQ_PositiveMood_",
              Transcendence = "^MEQ_Transcendence_", Ineffability = "^MEQ_Ineffability_"),
            function(p) alpha(items(p)))
a2 <- function(k) sprintf("%.2f", a[[k]])
```

Psychological flexibility was measured with the seven-item Acceptance and Action Questionnaire-II [AAQ-II; @bond2011preliminary; French version by @monestes2009french]. Its score is the sum of the items, each rated from 1 to 7, and a higher score means *less* flexibility (Cronbach's α in this sample = `r a2("AAQ")`, as for the values that follow). Distress was measured with the 21-item Depression Anxiety Stress Scales [DASS-21; @lovibond1995manual]. Each subscale score is the mean of its seven items, rated from 0 to 3, and the total is the mean of the three subscales (α = `r a2("DASS")` for the total, `r a2("Depression")`, `r a2("Anxiety")` and `r a2("Stress")` for Depression, Anxiety and Stress). Users also rated their last classic psychedelic experience on the 30-item Mystical Experience Questionnaire [MEQ-30; @barrett2015validation; @maclean2012factor]. The total and the four factor scores are means of the items, rated from 0 to 5 (α = `r a2("MEQ")` for the total, `r a2("Mystical")`, `r a2("PositiveMood")`, `r a2("Transcendence")` and `r a2("Ineffability")` for mystical experience, positive mood, transcendence of time and space, and ineffability). A scale was scored when at most one of its items was missing, as the mean of the answered items.

## Data Cleaning

The data preprocessing followed that of a larger modelling study of the same task (<https://github.com/RealityBending/IllusionGameComputational>), which also provided the priors described below.

```{r}
#| label: cleaning
open_trials <- read.csv(file.path(root, "data/open/illusiongame.csv"))
open_trials <- open_trials[open_trials$Participant %in% groups$Participant & open_trials$Block != "Practice", ]
bad_rt <- is.na(open_trials$RT) | open_trials$RT <= 0 | open_trials$RT >= 6000
kept <- open_trials[!bad_rt, ]
block <- paste(kept$Participant, kept$Illusion_Type, kept$Block)
facilitating <- kept$Illusion_Strength <= 0
block_error <- tapply(kept$Error[facilitating], block[facilitating], mean)
bad_blocks <- names(block_error)[block_error >= 1 / 3]
n_block_removed <- sum(block %in% bad_blocks)
stopifnot(sum(!block %in% bad_blocks) == n_trials)
# The same per group, in the order naive, past, recent. No trial has a missing
# or null response time: all those removed are slow. Every removed block is of
# the Ebbinghaus illusion.
trial_group <- factor(groups$Group[match(open_trials$Participant, groups$Participant)], levels = names(group_col))
block_group <- factor(groups$Group[match(sub(" .*", "", bad_blocks), groups$Participant)], levels = names(group_col))
stopifnot(!anyNA(open_trials$RT), open_trials$RT > 0, grepl(" Ebbinghaus ", bad_blocks), !anyNA(trial_group))
three <- function(x) paste0(x[1], ", ", x[2], " and ", x[3])
rt_by_group <- three(table(trial_group[bad_rt]))
blocks_by_group <- three(table(block_group))
```

As in that study, trials with a response time of six seconds or more were removed (`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * mean(bad_rt))`% of the trials). The other atypical responses, fast or slow, were left to the mixture component of the model described below. A participant's block of one illusion was removed when the error rate on its facilitating trials reached one third. Errors are rare on these trials (`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * median(block_error))`% in the median block, and at most `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * quantile(block_error, 0.95))`% in 95% of the blocks), so such a rate indicates that the block was not done as instructed, for instance with the keys reversed.

This removed `r sum(bad_rt)` trials for their response time (`r rt_by_group` in naïve participants, past users and recent users) and `r n_block_removed` trials in `r length(bad_blocks)` blocks (`r blocks_by_group` blocks, all of the Ebbinghaus illusion), and left `r format(n_trials, big.mark = ",")` trials from `r length(unique(trials$Participant))` participants.

## Data Analysis

### The Model

The task is a speeded choice between two alternatives which can be modelled in terms of evidence accumulation [@ratcliff2008diffusion], with the illusion adding a graded conflict [@ulrich2015automatic]. The choice and the response time of every trial were modelled jointly with a drift diffusion model [@ratcliff2008diffusion], which @fig-model A illustrates. After a non-decision time $\tau$, which covers encoding the stimulus and executing the response, evidence accumulates noisily between two boundaries, one for the correct response and one for the error, until it reaches one of them, which determines the decision. The model has five parameters. The *drift rate* $v$ is the average rate at which the evidence moves towards the correct response; it is negative when the evidence favours the error. The *boundary separation* $a$ is the amount of evidence gathered before responding: wider boundaries make responses slower and errors rarer, so it measures caution. The *start point* $w$ is where the accumulation begins, as a share of $a$ from the correct boundary (0.5 is unbiased). The *non-decision time* $\tau$ is the time outside the decision, and the *drift variability* $s_v$ is the standard deviation of the drift rate across trials [@ratcliff2008diffusion]. The trial-to-trial ranges of the start point and of the non-decision time were fixed to zero.

Each parameter had the same linear predictor. For each illusion it had an intercept, a slope on illusion strength, a slope on task difficulty and their interaction, and each of these terms could differ between the groups (Naïve, Past, Recent; treatment-coded, with Naïve as the reference). Participants had random effects: all twelve of these terms (four per illusion) for the drift rate, and one intercept per illusion for the four other parameters, with a correlation matrix per parameter. A small mixture component captured atypical responses, such as anticipations and lapses. Its probability had an intercept and a participant random intercept, and no group term.

The priors for the naïve group, the reference, came from that larger study's hierarchical fits of the same model to about 2,200 participants per illusion. For the Ebbinghaus and Müller-Lyer illusions, the intercepts, the slopes on strength and difficulty and their interaction, and the standard deviations of the participant effects were centred on that study's estimates, with prior standard deviations wide enough to allow for a different population. The vertical-horizontal illusion, for which no comparable fit was available, took the average of the two with twice the prior standard deviation. The coefficients for the group differences had weak priors centred on zero, normal(0, 2.5) for the drift rate and the software's defaults for the other parameters, because these differences are what the study estimates.

The model was fitted with brms 2.21 [@burkner2017brms] and the cogmod 0.3.6 family [@makowski2026cogmod] in Stan [@carpenter2017stan], on a computing cluster. Eight chains, each with 1,500 warm-up and 1,000 retained iterations, gave 8,000 draws. <!-- Diagnostics typed by hand from the 117-participant 8-chain fit of 2026-11-22 (population level: analysis/3_ddm_groups.qmd, "Loading"; participant level: the largest Rhat of the r_ parameters, AGENTS.md, DDM-5 entry). --> There were no divergent transitions. At the population level, the largest $\widehat{R}$ was 1.022 (4 of 181 coefficients above the recommended 1.01) and the smallest bulk effective sample size 494, above the recommended 400 [@vehtari2021rank]. At the participant level, the largest $\widehat{R}$ was 1.033.

### Indices

Posterior distributions were summarised by their median, their 95% equal-tailed interval and their probability of direction (*pd*), the share of draws with the same sign as the median [@makowski2019indices]. We describe a difference as reliable when its 95% interval excludes zero, that is, when its *pd* is at least 0.975. *Discriminability* is the drift rate $v$: the larger it is, the more strongly the evidence favours the correct response. The *probability of an error* is the probability that the accumulation reaches the error boundary first. It follows from the drift rate, the boundary separation and the start point, and was averaged over the trial-to-trial variability of the drift rate.

Three kinds of contrast answer the study's questions. For *general performance*, each quantity was averaged over the whole design, that is, over every combination of strength and difficulty that the task showed, for each illusion and across the three. The *effect of the illusion* is the change in a quantity from no illusion (strength 0) to the strongest conflicting illusion (strength 1), at mid difficulty. For the parameters, this is their slope on illusion strength, computed with `estimate_slopes()`. The third contrast is the *illusion magnitude*, defined as the effect of illusion strength on discriminability relative to the effect of task difficulty. It is computed from two slopes of discriminability, both taken at no illusion and mid difficulty, where $v(s, d)$ is the drift rate at strength $s$ and difficulty $d$. The first is the slope on illusion strength, $b_s = v(1, 0) - v(0, 0)$: how much discriminability the strongest conflicting illusion removes. The second is the slope on task difficulty, $b_d = v(0, 1) - v(0, 0)$: how much discriminability is lost per unit of difficulty. Both slopes are negative. Their ratio, $b_s / b_d$, is the number of units of task difficulty that one unit of illusion strength is worth. It corresponds to the shift of the point of subjective equality, expressed in the units of the task. This ratio is independent from overall task performance.

### Participant-level Analyses

Correlations between illusions were computed across participants. To assess what the covariates account for, each participant's index, averaged over the three illusions, was regressed on Group alone; on Group and age; on Group, age, native language and student status; and on Group and each questionnaire score. The MEQ-30 regressions include users only and so compare Recent with Past. Two further regressions, also on users only, asked whether the indices follow psychedelic use by degree, which the split at 30 days cannot show. The first was on the time since the last use (the logarithm of the number of days, alone and with age), and the second on Group and the lifetime number of uses (the six answer categories from one time to more than 100 times, scored 1 to 6). For each draw, the regression coefficients were themselves drawn from their sampling distribution, so that the intervals carry both the uncertainty of the participant estimates and that of a regression on about a hundred people. Native language and student status are each largely confined to one group, which limits what adjusting for them can show.


## Transparency and openness

The study was not preregistered. We collected as much data as we could until the data were frozen, and every exclusion is reported. Every estimate is given with its uncertainty, as a posterior median with its 95% interval, and the hierarchical Bayesian model carries the uncertainty of each participant's estimates into the group comparisons. The de-identified data, the analysis code and the reports from which every number in this article is read are at <https://github.com/RealityBending/IllusionGameSelfAssociation>.

B: the error rate and the median response time of each group across illusion strength, pooled over task difficulty and participants: observed (crosses), and the model's posterior predictive mean (lines) and 95% interval (bands). Each value pools two neighbouring strengths, which together cover all eight real differences. Positive strengths are conflicting: they push towards the error."

## General Performance

@fig-data B shows each group's error rate and median response time across illusion strength, together with the model's predictions, which follow the observed values closely. Users did the task differently from naïve participants, even when the illusion was weakest. Averaged over the whole design and the three illusions (@fig-model B), both user groups set wider boundaries than naïve participants (Past − Naïve `r fmt(avg("boundary", "Past - Never"))`; Recent − Naïve `r fmt(avg("boundary", "Recent - Never"))`): they gathered more evidence before responding. They made fewer errors (`r pts(avg("perror", "Past - Never"))` and `r pts(avg("perror", "Recent - Never"))`), and their non-decision time was slightly longer, though not reliably so (`r ms(avg("ndt", "Past - Never"))` and `r ms(avg("ndt", "Recent - Never"))`). Recent users also discriminated the targets better than naïve participants (drift rate: `r fmt(avg("delta", "Recent - Never"))`) and than past users (Recent − Past `r fmt(avg("delta", "Recent - Past"))`), whereas past users did not reliably differ from naïve participants (`r fmt(avg("delta", "Past - Never"))`). The start point and the drift variability did not differ between the groups.

@fig-model A illustrates the model with the group-level parameters of each group (those of a participant whose individual deviations from the group are null) at one condition, the strongest conflicting Ebbinghaus illusion at mid difficulty. How the model reproduces the data of all participants is shown in @fig-data B. In the naïve group, the drift rate points towards the error (`r minus(sprintf("%.2f", ddm_par["Never", "delta"]))`), and `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * ddm_par["Never", "perror"])` of the trials end in an error. In past and recent users, it points slightly towards the correct response (`r sprintf("%.2f", ddm_par["Past", "delta"])` and `r sprintf("%.2f", ddm_par["Recent", "delta"])`), and their boundaries are further apart (`r sprintf("%.2f", ddm_par["Past", "boundary"])` and `r sprintf("%.2f", ddm_par["Recent", "boundary"])`, against `r sprintf("%.2f", ddm_par["Never", "boundary"])`), so that fewer of their trials end in an error (`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * ddm_par["Past", "perror"])` and `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * ddm_par["Recent", "perror"])`) and their responses take longer.

```{r}
#| label: fig-model
#| apa-twocolumn: true
#| fig-cap: "A: the model at one condition, the strongest conflicting Ebbinghaus illusion at mid difficulty, with each group's group-level parameters (posterior medians). After the non-decision time, the evidence starts between the correct boundary (top) and the error boundary (bottom), and drifts noisily until it reaches one of them, which determines the decision. The thick line is the average drift, and the shaded fan around it spans the middle half of the trials' drift rates; the thin lines are three simulated trials. The densities beyond the boundaries are the resulting distributions of correct and of error response times, each scaled by its share of responses. Dashed grey lines repeat the naïve group. B: the model's parameters and derived quantities per group, averaged over the whole design and the three illusions. C: the illusion magnitude per group and illusion, that is, the number of units of task difficulty that one unit of illusion strength is worth (the strength slope of discriminability divided by its difficulty slope, at no illusion and mid difficulty). B and C: posterior medians and 95% intervals. Brackets mark the group differences with a probability of direction of at least 0.975 (one asterisk), 0.995 (two) or 0.9995 (three), the Bayesian counterparts of p < .05, .01 and .001."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 7.4
# A: the diffusion at one condition (the strongest conflicting Ebbinghaus
# illusion, mid difficulty), from the posterior medians of the group-level
# parameters (ddm_par, setup chunk). The evidence runs between the correct
# boundary, drawn on top at +a/2, and the error boundary at -a/2. It starts
# w * a below the correct boundary after the non-decision time, and drifts
# towards the correct boundary at v (= delta, the drift towards the correct
# response), which varies across trials with SD sv.
grp <- names(group_col)
as_group <- function(g) factor(g, levels = grp)
ddm_xmax <- 2.2      # s
ddm_k <- 0.6         # height of one unit of density, in evidence units
half <- qnorm(0.75)  # the fan: the middle half of the trials' drift rates
rt <- seq(0.005, ddm_xmax, by = 0.005)
geo <- lapply(setNames(grp, grp), function(g) {
  a <- ddm_par[g, ]
  list(top = a[["boundary"]] / 2, bottom = -a[["boundary"]] / 2,
       start = a[["boundary"]] / 2 - a[["bias"]] * a[["boundary"]],
       v = a[["delta"]], sv = a[["sigmadrift"]], ndt = a[["ndt"]])
})
# Response-time densities (cogmod's first-passage densities; response 0 is
# the correct boundary, 1 the error one), drawn beyond each boundary.
ddm_dens <- do.call(rbind, lapply(grp, function(g) {
  a <- ddm_par[g, ]
  f <- function(r) cogmod::dcogmod_ddm(rt, drift = a[["mu"]], boundary = a[["boundary"]], bias = a[["bias"]],
                                       ndt = a[["ndt"]], response = r, sigmadrift = a[["sigmadrift"]])
  p <- geo[[g]]
  rbind(data.frame(Group = as_group(g), Response = "Correct", RT = rt, y = p$top + ddm_k * f(0), base = p$top),
        data.frame(Group = as_group(g), Response = "Error", RT = rt, y = p$bottom - ddm_k * f(1), base = p$bottom))
}))
# Where a straight path from the start point at slope s meets a boundary (or
# the right edge).
ray_end <- function(p, s) {
  t_hit <- ifelse(s > 0, (p$top - p$start) / s, ifelse(s < 0, (p$bottom - p$start) / s, Inf))
  t_end <- pmin(p$ndt + t_hit, ddm_xmax)
  data.frame(x = t_end, y = p$start + s * (t_end - p$ndt))
}
ddm_drift <- do.call(rbind, lapply(grp, function(g) {
  p <- geo[[g]]
  data.frame(Group = as_group(g), x0 = p$ndt, y0 = p$start, ray_end(p, p$v))
}))
ddm_fan <- do.call(rbind, lapply(grp, function(g) {
  p <- geo[[g]]
  ends <- ray_end(p, seq(p$v - half * p$sv, p$v + half * p$sv, length.out = 40))
  data.frame(Group = as_group(g), x = c(p$ndt, ends$x), y = c(p$start, ends$y))
}))
ddm_bounds <- do.call(rbind, lapply(grp, function(g) {
  p <- geo[[g]]
  data.frame(Group = as_group(g), y = c(p$top, p$bottom))
}))
ddm_ndt <- do.call(rbind, lapply(grp, function(g) data.frame(Group = as_group(g), ndt = geo[[g]]$ndt, start = geo[[g]]$start)))
# Three simulated trials per group: a drift drawn from Normal(v, sv), then
# unit-variance noise in 2 ms steps until a boundary. Illustrative only.
set.seed(7)
ddm_paths <- do.call(rbind, lapply(grp, function(g) {
  p <- geo[[g]]
  do.call(rbind, lapply(1:3, function(i) {
    vi <- stats::rnorm(1, p$v, p$sv)
    dt <- 0.002
    y <- p$start
    t <- p$ndt
    while (y[length(y)] < p$top && y[length(y)] > p$bottom && t[length(t)] < ddm_xmax) {
      y <- c(y, y[length(y)] + vi * dt + sqrt(dt) * stats::rnorm(1))
      t <- c(t, t[length(t)] + dt)
    }
    data.frame(Group = as_group(g), id = paste(g, i), x = t, y = pmin(pmax(y, p$bottom), p$top))
  }))
}))
ddm_err <- data.frame(Group = as_group(grp), label = sprintf("%.0f%% errors", 100 * ddm_par[grp, "perror"]),
                      y = sapply(geo, `[[`, "bottom") - 0.95)
# The naive group, repeated in the two user panels as a dashed grey outline.
as_naive <- function(d) {
  d <- d[d$Group == "Never", ]
  do.call(rbind, lapply(c("Past", "Recent"), function(g) { d$Group <- as_group(g); d }))
}
p_never <- geo[["Never"]]
ddm_lab <- data.frame(Group = as_group("Never"),
                      x = c(0.02, 0.02, 0.02, 1.05),
                      y = c(p_never$top + 0.95, p_never$bottom - 0.95, p_never$start + 0.45, p_never$top - 0.3),
                      label = c("Correct responses", "Errors", "Non-decision\ntime (τ)", "Drift rate (v)"))
p_ddm <- ggplot() +
  geom_hline(data = as_naive(ddm_bounds), aes(yintercept = y), colour = group_col[["Never"]], linewidth = 0.3, linetype = "31") +
  geom_line(data = as_naive(ddm_dens), aes(RT, y, group = Response), colour = group_col[["Never"]], linewidth = 0.3, linetype = "31") +
  geom_hline(data = ddm_bounds, aes(yintercept = y, colour = Group), linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_ribbon(data = ddm_dens, aes(RT, ymin = pmin(base, y), ymax = pmax(base, y), fill = Group, group = Response), alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(data = ddm_dens, aes(RT, y, colour = Group, group = Response), linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_polygon(data = ddm_fan, aes(x, y, fill = Group, group = Group), alpha = 0.18) +
  geom_path(data = ddm_paths, aes(x, y, colour = Group, group = id), linewidth = 0.15, alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_segment(data = as_naive(ddm_ndt), aes(x = 0, xend = ndt, y = start, yend = start), colour = group_col[["Never"]], linewidth = 0.3, linetype = "31") +
  geom_segment(data = as_naive(ddm_drift), aes(x = x0, xend = x, y = y0, yend = y), colour = group_col[["Never"]], linewidth = 0.3, linetype = "31") +
  geom_segment(data = ddm_drift, aes(x = x0, xend = x, y = y0, yend = y, colour = Group), linewidth = 0.7,
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.07, "in"), angle = 25, type = "closed")) +
  geom_segment(data = ddm_ndt, aes(x = 0, xend = ndt, y = start, yend = start, colour = Group), linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(data = ddm_ndt, aes(ndt, start, colour = Group), size = 1.1) +
  geom_text(data = ddm_err, aes(x = ddm_xmax - 0.03, y = y, label = label, colour = Group), hjust = 1, size = 2.6) +
  geom_text(data = ddm_lab, aes(x, y, label = label), hjust = 0, size = 2.3, colour = "#55554f", lineheight = 0.95) +
  facet_wrap(~ Group, nrow = 1, labeller = as_labeller(group_lab)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = group_col, guide = "none") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = group_col, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 2, 0.5), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.01))) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = NULL) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, ddm_xmax), ylim = c(min(ddm_err$y) - 0.15, max(sapply(geo, `[[`, "top")) + 1.1)) +
  labs(x = "Time from stimulus onset (s)", y = "Evidence", subtitle = "Ebbinghaus illusion, strongest conflicting strength") +
  theme_paper +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), panel.spacing.x = unit(0.8, "lines"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 8, colour = "#55554f"))

# Group values as dots and intervals, with a bracket for every contrast with
# pd >= 0.975: Never-Past and Past-Recent in a first column, Never-Recent in a
# second. The x axis keeps room on the right for them, without breaks there.
dots_groups <- function(values, contrasts, xlab = NULL) {
  lv <- rev(names(group_col))  # bottom to top
  values$Group <- factor(values$Group, levels = lv)
  hi <- tapply(values$CI_high, values$Panel, max)
  lo <- tapply(values$CI_low, values$Panel, min)
  span <- hi - lo
  room <- 0.3
  reserve <- data.frame(Panel = factor(names(hi), levels = levels(values$Panel)), x = hi + room * span)
  p <- ggplot(values, aes(Median, Group)) +
    geom_blank(data = reserve, aes(x = x), inherit.aes = FALSE) +
    geom_linerange(aes(xmin = CI_low, xmax = CI_high, colour = Group), linewidth = 0.6) +
    geom_point(aes(colour = Group), size = 1.8) +
    facet_wrap(~ Panel, scales = "free_x", nrow = 1) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = group_col, guide = "none") +
    scale_y_discrete(labels = group_lab) +
    scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.02)), breaks = function(l) {
      top <- l[1] + diff(l) / (1 + room)
      b <- scales::breaks_extended(4)(c(l[1], top))
      b[b <= top]
    }) +
    labs(x = xlab, y = NULL) +
    theme_paper + theme(panel.spacing.x = unit(1, "lines"))
  br <- contrasts[contrasts$pd >= 0.975, ]
  if (nrow(br)) {
    ends <- do.call(rbind, strsplit(as.character(br$Contrast), " - ", fixed = TRUE))
    y1 <- match(ends[, 1], lv); y2 <- match(ends[, 2], lv)
    br$ymin <- pmin(y1, y2) + 0.12; br$ymax <- pmax(y1, y2) - 0.12
    pn <- as.character(br$Panel)
    br$x <- hi[pn] + span[pn] * ifelse(abs(y1 - y2) == 2, 0.19, 0.07)
    br$tick <- 0.025 * span[pn]
    br$Stars <- stars(br$pd)
    # The stars run along the bracket (rotated), so they take little width.
    p <- p +
      geom_segment(data = br, aes(x = x, xend = x, y = ymin, yend = ymax), inherit.aes = FALSE, colour = "#444444", linewidth = 0.35) +
      geom_segment(data = br, aes(x = x - tick, xend = x, y = ymin, yend = ymin), inherit.aes = FALSE, colour = "#444444", linewidth = 0.35) +
      geom_segment(data = br, aes(x = x - tick, xend = x, y = ymax, yend = ymax), inherit.aes = FALSE, colour = "#444444", linewidth = 0.35) +
      geom_text(data = br, aes(x = x, y = (ymin + ymax) / 2, label = Stars), inherit.aes = FALSE,
                angle = 90, hjust = 0.5, vjust = 1.4, size = 3, colour = "#444444")
  }
  p
}
panel_lab <- c(boundary = "Boundary separation", ndt = "Non-decision time (s)", delta = "Discriminability", perror = "P(error)")
general_m <- avg_means[avg_means$Illusion_Type == "All" & avg_means$Quantity %in% names(panel_lab), ]
general_m$Panel <- factor(panel_lab[general_m$Quantity], levels = panel_lab)
general_c <- averaged[averaged$Illusion_Type == "All" & averaged$Quantity %in% names(panel_lab), ]
general_c$Panel <- factor(panel_lab[general_c$Quantity], levels = panel_lab)
index_m <- slopes[slopes$Quantity == "index" & !is.na(slopes$Group), ]
index_m$Panel <- factor(illusions[index_m$Illusion_Type], levels = illusions)
index_c <- slopes[slopes$Quantity == "index" & !is.na(slopes$Contrast), ]
index_c$Panel <- factor(illusions[index_c$Illusion_Type], levels = illusions)
p_general <- dots_groups(general_m, general_c)
p_index <- dots_groups(index_m, index_c, xlab = "Illusion magnitude (difficulty units per unit of strength)")
save_figure((p_ddm / p_general / p_index) + plot_layout(heights = c(1.9, 1, 1.1)) + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A"),
            "Figure2", width = 7, height = 7.4)
```

## Illusion Sensitivity

@fig-model C shows the illusion magnitude of each group, the measure of illusion sensitivity that does not depend on overall performance. In the naïve group, one unit of illusion strength was worth `r sprintf("%.2f", idx("Never", "Ebbinghaus")$Median)`, `r sprintf("%.2f", idx("Never", "MullerLyer")$Median)` and `r sprintf("%.2f", idx("Never", "VerticalHorizontal")$Median)` units of task difficulty on the Ebbinghaus, Müller-Lyer and vertical-horizontal illusions: the strongest conflicting illusion lowered discriminability as much as moving that far along the difficulty scale, whose whole range spans 2 units. The magnitude was lower in both user groups on every illusion, by `r round(min(idx_pct))` to `r round(max(idx_pct))`% of the naïve value (`r round(mean(idx_pct))`% on average). Taken one illusion at a time, the 95% intervals of all six differences excluded zero (@tbl-scales). Averaged over the three illusions, participants' magnitudes were lower in both user groups (Past − Naïve `r fmt(cov("Illusion magnitude (strength / difficulty)", "Group", "Past - Never"))`; Recent − Naïve `r fmt(cov("Illusion magnitude (strength / difficulty)", "Group", "Recent - Never"))`). Recent and past users did not differ (Recent − Past `r med_rng(idx_all("Recent - Past"))` across illusions).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-scales
#| apa-twocolumn: true
#| tbl-cap: "The illusion's effect in users relative to naïve participants, on three measures."
#| apa-note: "Posterior median [95% interval] of the difference between the groups. P(error) and discriminability: the difference in the change from no illusion to the strongest conflicting illusion, at mid difficulty. A negative value on P(error) means that the illusion adds fewer errors in users; a negative value on discriminability means that it removes more discriminability in users. Illusion magnitude: the difference in the number of units of task difficulty that one unit of illusion strength is worth; a negative value means that the illusion is equivalent to a smaller real difference in users."
ts <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("Past - Never", "Recent - Never"), function(cn) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(illusions), function(il) {
    data.frame(Contrast = contrast_lab[[cn]], Illusion = illusions[[il]],
               "P(error)" = fmt(eff("perror", cn, il)),
               "Discriminability" = fmt(eff("delta", cn, il)),
               "Illusion magnitude" = fmt(idx_c(cn, il)), check.names = FALSE)
  }))
}))
knitr::kable(ts, row.names = FALSE)
```

The two other measures of the illusion's effect depend on overall performance (@tbl-scales). In discriminability, the strongest conflicting illusion cost users about as much as naïve participants: the group differences were small and their intervals included zero on every illusion (Past − Naïve `r med_rng(eff_all("delta", "Past - Never"))` across illusions; Recent − Naïve `r med_rng(eff_all("delta", "Recent - Never"))`). In errors, the same illusions cost users less on the Ebbinghaus illusion, where they added `r sprintf("%.0f and %.0f", -100 * eff("perror", "Past - Never", "Ebbinghaus")$Median, -100 * eff("perror", "Recent - Never", "Ebbinghaus")$Median)` points fewer errors in past and recent users. They cost them somewhat less on the vertical-horizontal illusion (`r sprintf("%.0f and %.0f", -100 * eff("perror", "Past - Never", "VerticalHorizontal")$Median, -100 * eff("perror", "Recent - Never", "VerticalHorizontal")$Median)` points fewer, with intervals that included zero), and about as much on the Müller-Lyer illusion, which at its strongest brings every group to the same error rate. Users' discriminability thus dropped as much with the illusion as naïve participants', but more with task difficulty, which is why their illusion magnitude was smaller.

## Across Illusions

Do the three illusions measure one common sensitivity to illusions? Across participants, the illusion magnitude was moderately correlated between illusions (Ebbinghaus and Müller-Lyer `r cor_mag("Ebbinghaus & Müller-Lyer")`; Ebbinghaus and vertical-horizontal `r cor_mag("Ebbinghaus & Vertical-Horizontal")`; Müller-Lyer and vertical-horizontal `r cor_mag("Müller-Lyer & Vertical-Horizontal")`). General performance was more strongly shared: the discriminability with no illusion correlated from `r med_rng(correlations$Median[correlations$Quantity == "Discriminability, no illusion"])` between illusions. The illusions thus share part of their sensitivity, but less than they share general performance.

## Age, Demographics, Questionnaires and Psychedelic Use

Age accounted for the users' slightly longer non-decision time, which increased by `r ms(cov("Non-decision time (s), no illusion", "Group + age", "Age (per 10 years)"))` per decade of age. With age in the regression, the Past − Naïve difference went from `r minus(sprintf("%+.0f", 1000 * cov("Non-decision time (s), no illusion", "Group", "Past - Never")$Median))` to `r ms(cov("Non-decision time (s), no illusion", "Group + age", "Past - Never"))`, and the Recent − Naïve difference from `r minus(sprintf("%+.0f", 1000 * cov("Non-decision time (s), no illusion", "Group", "Recent - Never")$Median))` to `r ms(cov("Non-decision time (s), no illusion", "Group + age", "Recent - Never"))`. Age did not account for the users' wider boundaries (with age in the regression: Past − Naïve `r fmt(cov("Boundary, no illusion", "Group + age", "Past - Never"))`; Recent − Naïve `r fmt(cov("Boundary, no illusion", "Group + age", "Recent - Never"))`), nor for their smaller illusion magnitude, which did not change with age (`r fmt(cov("Illusion magnitude (strength / difficulty)", "Group + age", "Age (per 10 years)"), 3)` per decade). Its group differences stayed the same with age, native language and student status in the regression (Past − Naïve `r fmt(cov("Illusion magnitude (strength / difficulty)", "Group + age + native + student", "Past - Never"))`, Recent − Naïve `r fmt(cov("Illusion magnitude (strength / difficulty)", "Group + age + native + student", "Recent - Never"))`). The illusion magnitude was unrelated to the AAQ-II (`r fmt(cov("Illusion magnitude (strength / difficulty)", "Group + AAQ-II", "AAQ-II (per SD)"), 3)` per standard deviation), the DASS-21 (`r fmt(cov("Illusion magnitude (strength / difficulty)", "Group + DASS-21", "DASS-21 (per SD)"), 3)`) and, among users, the MEQ-30 total (`r fmt(cov("Illusion magnitude (strength / difficulty)", "Group + MEQ-30 total (users)", "MEQ-30 total (per SD)"), 3)`) or any of its four factors. Higher AAQ-II and DASS-21 scores went only with a slightly shorter non-decision time (`r ms(cov("Non-decision time (s), no illusion", "Group + AAQ-II", "AAQ-II (per SD)"))` and `r ms(cov("Non-decision time (s), no illusion", "Group + DASS-21", "DASS-21 (per SD)"))` per standard deviation), and, among users, a higher MEQ-30 total with a slightly longer one (`r ms(cov("Non-decision time (s), no illusion", "Group + MEQ-30 total (users)", "MEQ-30 total (per SD)"))`). None of these covariates accounted for the users' wider boundaries.

Among users, the illusion magnitude did not reliably follow the time since the last use (`r fmt(use_days("Illusion magnitude (strength / difficulty)"), 3)` per tenfold increase in the number of days) or the lifetime number of uses (`r fmt(use_life("Illusion magnitude (strength / difficulty)"), 3)` per answer category), and neither did the boundary separation (`r fmt(use_days("Boundary, no illusion"))` and `r fmt(use_life("Boundary, no illusion"))`). Discriminability with no illusion changed by `r fmt(use_days("Discriminability, no illusion"))` per tenfold increase in the time since the last use, and by `r fmt(use_life("Discriminability, no illusion"))` per category of lifetime use.

# Discussion

We asked whether people who use classic psychedelics differ from psychedelic-naïve adults in their susceptibility to visual illusions outside the acute state. Adults who had used a classic psychedelic differed from psychedelic-naïve adults on the Illusion Game in two ways, which we tried to disentangle. First, they performed the task differently overall. They set wider decision boundaries, gathering more evidence before responding, and made fewer errors, with or without an illusion. Second, they were somewhat less sensitive to the illusions. Their illusion magnitude, the effect of illusion strength on performance relative to the effect of the real difference, was `r round(mean(idx_pct))`% lower than that of naïve participants on average (`r round(min(idx_pct))`–`r round(max(idx_pct))`% across illusions). Neither difference distinguished people who had used a psychedelic in the last month from people who had used one longer ago.

The first difference, in the decision boundaries, is the larger one, and is not an effect of the illusions. In the model, it is a matter of caution: users required more evidence before responding, so they responded later and erred less. Age is an obvious candidate explanation. Both user groups were about twelve years older than the naïve group, and older adults have been reported to set wider boundaries and to have longer non-decision times [@ratcliff2001effects; @theisen2021age]. In our regressions, age accounted for the users' slightly longer non-decision time and for part of the past users' lower error rate, whereas its estimated effect on the boundaries (`r fmt(cov("Boundary, no illusion", "Group + age", "Age (per 10 years)"))` per decade) was small relative to the difference between the groups. This does not rule age out. Its effect is estimated from the variation of age within the groups, which is limited: only one of the `r n_group[["Never"]]` naïve participants was aged 31 to 50, against `r age_mid[["Recent"]]` of the `r n_group[["Recent"]]` recent users. Earlier comparisons of users with non-users on neuropsychological tests found no uniform difference, and better performance in some samples [@basedow2021neuropsychological; @bouso2012personality]. Better performance in users is thus not without precedent, though those comparisons share the confounds of this one. The one general difference between the two user groups was a higher discriminability in recent users, with or without an illusion. None of the other differences was explained by age, language, student status, psychological flexibility, distress or the reported intensity of the last experience.

The second difference is the one that bears on the predictive-processing account, with three indices used to describe it (@tbl-scales). The first is the illusion's effect on discriminability, which measures how much the illusory context reduces the drift of the evidence towards the correct response. This effect did not differ between the groups: the illusion cost users as much discriminability as naïve participants. Users' discriminability, however, changed more with the real difference between the targets, so that the same illusory effect weighed less against it. The second is the illusion's effect on errors, which measures how often the illusion turns a correct judgement into an error. This effect was smaller in users on the Ebbinghaus illusion, less clearly so on the vertical-horizontal illusion, and similar on the Müller-Lyer illusion. Only the Ebbinghaus illusion, then, reliably led users to the wrong answer less often. The third is the illusion magnitude, which expresses the illusion's effect as the real difference between the targets that it is equivalent to, like the shift of the point of subjective equality in psychophysics. It was smaller in both user groups, on every illusion, which suggests that users' perception of the targets was less biased by the illusion. The three indices thus answer different questions. The first two describe what the illusion does to the evidence and to the response, whereas the illusion magnitude describes the size of the perceptual bias, which is what REBUS makes predictions about. By this index, users were less sensitive to the illusions, and none of the covariates that we measured changed it.

Although this is the direction that REBUS predicts, the pattern across the groups was not what we expected. Recent users did not differ from past users in their sensitivity to the illusions, and the illusion magnitude was unrelated to the intensity of the last experience, to the time since it and to the lifetime number of uses. If priors relaxed for days after a dose and then recovered, the illusions would be smaller in recent users and not in past users. What we observe instead is a difference between a population of psychedelic users and a population of young controls, most of them students, whether the last use was weeks or years ago. One interpretation is that of a lasting change after psychedelic use. Enduring changes in personality, attitudes and well-being have been documented long after one or a few doses [@aday2020longterm; @knudsen2023sustained], and long-term ayahuasca users differed from matched controls in the thickness of the posterior cingulate cortex, to a degree that followed the intensity and duration of their use [@bouso2015longterm]. A lasting change in perception would be of the same kind. It would, however, be expected to grow with use, and we found no relation between the illusion magnitude and the lifetime number of uses. A second interpretation is that of a difference that was there before, in the people who choose to use psychedelics: in perceptual style, in familiarity with altered perception, or in how they approach a visual task. A third is that of some other difference between the two populations. Our cross-sectional design cannot tell them apart.

These results also differ from those of the acute studies. Under psilocybin the Ebbinghaus illusion became larger, not smaller [@aqil2025psilocybin], and experienced users did not differ from controls on a bodily illusion [@harduf2023bodily]. Our users were tested days to years after their last dose, and a different measure was used in each of these studies, so the results do not contradict one another. But together they give little support to a single account in which psychedelics weaken illusions by relaxing priors. Such an account would also need the three illusions to depend on priors to a similar degree, which is not established. Geometrical illusions have also been related to earlier stages of visual processing [@morgan1990biases; @schwarzkopf2011surface], although the relation with the surface area of the primary visual cortex was not replicated [@jastrzebowska2026neural]. Nor do they behave as one phenomenon. Susceptibility is typically only weakly correlated between illusions [@cretenoud2019factors; @jastrzebowska2026neural], even if some similarity between geometrical illusions has been reported [@axelrod2017perceptual], and susceptibility to the Müller-Lyer illusion, but not to the Ebbinghaus illusion, varies with autistic traits [@chouinard2013global] and with age during development [@navarrete2025heterochronic]. Our data agree. The illusion magnitude was only moderately correlated across the three illusions, and its reduction in users ranged from `r round(min(idx_pct_ill))`% on the `r illusions[[names(which.min(idx_pct_ill))]]` illusion to `r round(max(idx_pct_ill))`% on the `r illusions[[names(which.max(idx_pct_ill))]]` illusion. A difference between users and non-users may therefore not have the same origin for each illusion.

The study has several limitations. The design is cross-sectional, and the groups were recruited through different routes. Every difference between users and naïve participants is therefore confounded with age, education, language and whatever else draws a person to a psychedelic society. The groups overlap in age in only a few participants, so we did not adjust the model for age. Instead, we reported what age and the other covariates account for, and relied on the comparison of recent with past users, which holds them constant. The sample is modest and its size was not planned for a given power. Psychedelic use was self-reported and not verified, and the 30-day window groups together experiences with different substances, doses and settings. Testing was online, on displays that we did not control. The model reproduces the error rates and the median response times closely, but predicts a longer tail of slow errors than observed. Its boundary separation and start point were allowed to vary with illusion strength and task difficulty, like its other parameters, although the trials were mixed within blocks, so that participants could not set them for the coming trial. These terms may therefore absorb effects of the stimulus that the drift rate alone does not capture.

In sum, people who use classic psychedelics did this task more cautiously and more accurately than younger, psychedelic-naïve adults, and were somewhat less sensitive to the illusions, adjusting for perceptual performance. This second finding is in the direction that relaxed priors would predict, but it characterises the population of users and not the recent dose. Whether a dose produces it, and for how long, is a question for future within-subject designs that measure the illusion magnitude before and after.
